title: CEO Interview with Sunghyun Park of Rebellions - Semiwiki
gist: Rebellions, Korea's first AI-chip unicorn (~$850M raised, ~$2.3B valuation, pre-IPO), pitches dedicated inference silicon (REBEL100: Samsung 4nm chiplet, 144GB HBM3E, 2 PFLOPS FP8) plus an open software stack and rack/pod systems, arguing data centers are power-constrained and buyers now optimize tokens per watt and per dollar. Its demand pull comes from sovereign AI programs, telcos (KT Cloud) and a 100-rack Japan deployment, with Samsung, SK hynix and Arm as strategic partners and backers.

insights.claim: Rebellions argues AI's center of gravity has shifted from training to inference, because inference runs continuously for years while training happens once, changing the key buying metric to cost and power per token.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Supports the thesis that inference-specialized accelerators can take share from training-oriented GPUs as workloads mature.
insights.quote: The center of gravity in AI has moved from training to inference.

insights.claim: Data center operators are constrained by fixed megawatt power budgets rather than chip availability, so customers now ask for tokens per watt and per dollar instead of raw speed.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Power efficiency becomes a primary competitive axis for AI silicon; watch grid capacity as the binding constraint on AI buildout.
insights.quote: Most data centers aren’t short of chips. They’re short of power.
insights.locator: Most data centers aren't short of chips

insights.claim: As AI moves from pilots to production, CFOs are scrutinizing cost per token, and hardware that looked fine in demos can break the business case at scale.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: TCO pressure on production inference favors lower-cost, efficient alternatives to incumbent GPU deployments.
insights.locator: What keeps your customers up at night?

insights.claim: Customers want a credible second source to NVIDIA and minimal switching costs, including open-source-based software, reflecting supply and lock-in concerns.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Second-source demand is a tailwind for non-NVIDIA inference vendors; open-software compatibility is the key adoption gate.

insights.claim: Rebellions' second-generation REBEL100 inference chip is built on Samsung's 4nm process, uses a chiplet architecture with 144GB of HBM3E, and delivers 2 PFLOPS at FP8, which the company claims is the industry's first chiplet design with that HBM capacity.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Adds a Samsung 4nm/HBM3E design win and a data point on Samsung Foundry's leading-edge customer base.
insights.quote: It is the industry’s first chiplet architecture with 144GB of HBM3E, and it delivers 2 PFLOPS at FP8.
insights.locator: What application areas are your strongest?

insights.claim: Rebellions' RBLN SDK connects PyTorch, TensorFlow and Hugging Face to its NPUs with no retraining, serves models via vLLM, and scales from a single RebelServer to RebelRack and RebelPOD.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Software portability is positioned as the lever to reduce CUDA-style lock-in; adoption depends on day-one support for new open models.

insights.claim: Rebellions is shifting from selling chips to selling systems, having launched RebelRack (production inference compute unit) and RebelPOD (multi-rack cluster) in March, because customers want plug-in token-serving capacity rather than cards.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Mirrors the industry move to rack-scale sales, raising revenue per deal but also capital and integration demands for a startup.
insights.quote: Customers today don’t want a card.
insights.locator: What new features/technology are you working on?

insights.claim: Rebellions' next-generation silicon, in development, targets memory-centric architecture and AI-assisted hardware-software co-design, alongside ongoing investment in chiplet integration, memory bandwidth and scale-out networking.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Memory bandwidth remains the focal bottleneck for inference silicon, sustaining HBM demand.
insights.locator: Our next-generation silicon, now in development

insights.claim: Rebellions has raised about $850M in total, including a $400M pre-IPO round in March 2026 at roughly $2.3B valuation, and was the first recipient of Korea's National Growth Fund, with a public offering on the horizon.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: A likely upcoming Korean AI-chip IPO; state backing signals Korea treating inference silicon as strategic.
insights.locator: As South Korea's first AI chip unicorn

insights.claim: Rebellions' backers include Samsung, SK hynix, SK Telecom, KT, Arm and Aramco, and it works closely with Samsung Foundry, SK hynix for HBM, and Arm, giving it leading-edge process, memory and supply access unusual for a startup of its size.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Strategic investors double as supply chain and customers; HBM allocation access is a key moat versus other inference startups.

insights.claim: Rebellions is deployed in production with Korean telcos and cloud providers, with KT Cloud the first Korean cloud offering NPU-based AI services on its chips.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Early revenue base is concentrated in domestic Korean telco/cloud customers that are also investors.
insights.locator: We're deployed in production with Korea's telcos

insights.claim: Rebellions announced a 100-rack deployment in Japan with partner AI& supporting Japan's sovereign AI initiatives, and is expanding teams into the U.S., Japan, Singapore and the Middle East.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Sovereign AI programs are a demand channel for non-US AI silicon, creating regional openings outside NVIDIA's core hyperscaler base.

insights.claim: Rebellions argues the definition of sovereign AI is shifting: beyond data sovereignty and owning the stack, heterogeneous compute matters more than simply diversifying hardware.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Suggests sovereign buyers will fund mixed-architecture stacks, benefiting alternative accelerator vendors with open software.
insights.quote: heterogeneous compute matters more than simply diversifying HWs.

insights.claim: Rebellions concedes NVIDIA is the benchmark and will remain very important, but argues inference is a distinct market large enough to support dedicated architectures, competing also with hyperscaler in-house chips and well-funded startups.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Frames inference as a multi-vendor market; the specialized-player field (in-house ASICs, startups) is crowded, so differentiation claims need production proof.
insights.quote: NVIDIA is the benchmark and will remain very important.
insights.locator: What does the competitive landscape look like
